events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Arjun proposes Arjun, Isha. I know I am Good, and I have no information distinguishing the other players, so I’ll choose Isha for the first mission.

Arjun’s proposal of Arjun and Isha is a reasonable opening for a two-person mission: it is small, and Arjun explained his reasoning. I do not have information that distinguishes Isha from Felix or Amara, so I am not ready to accuse anyone based on this draft alone. I will judge the final team on whether the reasoning and discussion justify it.

Arjun’s proposal of Arjun and Isha is small and clearly explained. I know I am Good, but I have no information distinguishing Isha from Felix or Amara, so I cannot pretend to have a strong read on this draft. For now, I am not ready to accuse anyone based on the proposal alone. I will judge the final team on whether the discussion gives enough reason to trust it.

Arjun and Isha are the proposed team for Mission 1. Arjun gave a clear reason: it is a small opening team, and he says he knows he is Good. Isha has not yet spoken in this discussion, so from the public record I do not have a specific contradiction or accusation to make against either of them. I think the proposal is reasonable enough to evaluate on the final reasoning rather than reject it on the draft alone. I will judge the final team on whether the discussion gives enough reason to trust it.

Thanks, Elena, for laying out the reasoning on Arjun’s draft. I want to be clear about my own position: Arjun proposed Arjun and Isha for Mission 1, and I am Good, so I know at least one of the two slots on this team is clean from my side — I can vouch for myself. I have no private information that distinguishes Felix, Amara, or Elena from one another, so I will not pretend to a read I do not have. What matters to me is that Arjun’s stated rationale is the minimal-risk opening: a two-player team means only two cards, so if the mission succeeds it tells us little, but if it fails the information is concentrated. For a first mission I find that a sensible way to begin. I would rather we approve a modest, clearly explained team than force a larger team with unearned trust attached. If anyone has a concrete reason to believe Arjun or I am Evil, I would like to hear it stated plainly before the vote, rather than suspicion kept private. Otherwise I intend to judge this on the discussion as it stands.

I have no reason to doubt Arjun or Isha, so I am inclined to approve this two-player opening team. Arjun's reasoning is simple and keeps the information concentrated, which is a sensible way to start. I would rather we move to the vote on this team than keep restating the same points, and I will judge the result by how the mission turns out.

I will approve Arjun and Isha. Nothing in the discussion gives a concrete reason to suspect either of them, and a two-player mission is a low-risk way to gather information. Elena's last two statements mostly restate that she is Good and that she will judge the team later, without adding new reasoning, so I do not take them as a signal either way. I would rather we see the mission result than keep debating a draft that is already clear.

The discussion so far has been straightforward, and I appreciate that Felix and Elena are both reasoning openly rather than hiding suspicions. I have already stated my position: I am Good, I vouch for myself, and I see no reason from the public record to doubt Arjun as leader. My only note is that I would like to hear from Amara before we move to the vote, since everyone else on the team has weighed in. Amara, do you have any concerns about this two-player proposal, or are you comfortable approving Arjun and Isha for Mission 1?

Isha asked me directly, so I'll answer plainly: I have no concerns about this two-player proposal, and I am comfortable approving Arjun and Isha for Mission 1. Arjun's reasoning as leader was transparent — he knows his own alignment, had no information to distinguish the rest of us, and picked a minimal-risk opening team. That is exactly the kind of low-information, clearly justified choice I want to see from a first proposal. Isha has also stated her position openly and invited anyone with a concrete suspicion to bring it forward before the vote, which I appreciate; nothing of that kind has surfaced. On Elena's repeated statements: I read them as ordinary caution rather than a signal, and Felix already made the fair point that they don't change the picture either way. For my part, I have nothing concrete against anyone at this table, and I would rather not manufacture suspicion out of thin air on the first mission. If the team succeeds, we learn little but bank a mission; if it fails, the concentrated information is valuable. Either way, approving this team now gives us something real to work with instead of endless speculation. I'm ready to see this go to a vote.

I still approve Arjun and Isha for Mission 1. Nothing raised in this discussion gives a concrete reason to doubt either of them, and Amara's answer addresses the points that were raised. The team is small, the reasoning is clear, and the mission result will tell us more than further debate. I am ready for the vote.
Arjun confirms Arjun, Isha. No concrete concern emerged in discussion, so I will keep the original team.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Isha, Felix, Amara. Mission 2 requires a three-player team. I include myself since I was on the successful Mission 1 team and know I am Good, plus Felix and Amara, who both reasoned openly and clearly in the Mission 1 discussion and have not yet had cards submitted. This gives us two fresh reads while keeping one trusted anchor on the team.

Mission 1 succeeded, but that does not prove Isha is Good: an Evil player could have played Success. I know I am Good, so I would prefer a team with both Isha and me plus one new player. Including both Felix and Amara adds two untested players while leaving out someone from the successful team. Isha, what makes you prefer testing two new players over retaining both Mission 1 members?

Arjun raises a fair point: Mission 1 success does not clear anyone, since Evil can play Success to blend in. Let me answer his question directly. My reasoning for including Felix and Amara rather than Arjun comes down to information efficiency. If we keep both Mission 1 members on Mission 2, we learn nothing new about Felix, Amara, or Elena — three of us remain completely untested after two missions. With five players and two missions, one of them should cover new ground. I kept myself as the anchor: I was on Mission 1, I am Good, and I vouch for my own card. Felix and Amara both argued openly and reasonably in the Mission 1 discussion, and neither has submitted a card yet, so testing them now gives us maximum fresh information. Arjun, your argument that a team with both of us plus one new player would be safer is understandable, but it front-loads trust instead of evidence. On a team of three where I am already certain of one slot, adding one tested player and one untested player is the natural balance. I do not distrust you, Arjun — I would simply rather learn something about the rest of the table while we still have missions left to use that knowledge. If the mission fails, the concentrated information tells us a great deal about Felix and Amara. If it succeeds, we have tested two new players without risking a slot on someone with no proven track record.

Isha’s answer to Arjun is coherent: after one successful Mission 1, keeping both Arjun and Isha on Mission 2 would spend two slots on already-tested players and leave Felix, Amara, and me with no cards submitted. I know I am Good, but from the public record I have no concrete evidence distinguishing Felix or Amara; both spoke openly in the Mission 1 discussion. The proposed team adds two untested players while keeping one anchor from a successful mission. Arjun’s caution is fair, but it is not a concrete accusation against anyone on this team. I am inclined to approve Isha, Felix, and Amara and would rather see the mission result than extend the debate without new evidence.

Isha, I understand the desire to test more players, but a failure with both Felix and Amara aboard would be harder to interpret than a failure with just one new player. Also, retaining both Mission 1 members and adding one new player would still test someone new. Since I know I am Good, I prefer that team and am inclined to reject the current proposal.

Isha’s proposal is coherent. Keeping one Mission 1 anchor and testing two players who have not yet submitted cards is a reasonable way to gain information. I understand Arjun’s caution about interpretability, but it is not a concrete reason to reject Isha, Felix, or Amara. I am inclined to approve this team and see the mission result.

I'm not comfortable approving Isha, Felix, and Amara yet. I can vouch for myself as Good, and I'm not going to pretend to know more than I do about the others. My concern is Amara. When Isha asked her directly, she answered with a fast approval, called Elena's statements ordinary caution, and said she was ready to see this go to a vote. Felix's own earlier comment on Elena was that her repeated restatements didn't add new reasoning, but Amara's response went further by dismissing that caution and pushing the group toward a vote. With a threshold of one Fail card, a team with an untested player who is pressing for closure gives Evil an easy fail. Isha, would you be willing to replace Amara with Arjun? That keeps one tested Good anchor and still tests a new player, and it answers Arjun's concern about interpretability by leaving only one untested slot.

Felix raises a fair point about Amara's eagerness in Mission 1, and I appreciate that he voiced it directly rather than hiding it. But I want to be careful here: Amara's quick approval and readiness to vote could just as easily be the behavior of a Good player who saw a clean, well-reasoned proposal and didn't see a reason to manufacture suspicion. In a game where trust is scarce, expressing confidence early is not inherently Evil behavior — if it were, we'd be treating every player who votes yes as suspicious.

I also want to push back gently on the suggestion itself. Felix wants to replace Amara with Arjun. That would put both Mission 1 members back on the team plus one new player — exactly what Arjun advocated for in his earlier speech. If Felix is concerned about having two untested players on the team, swapping Amara for Arjun still leaves one untested player (Felix himself), so it doesn't actually solve the interpretability problem Arjun raised in a different way. And if the mission fails with Arjun and Isha aboard, we would be no better positioned than we are now to identify the Evil player among us, since both are already trusted.

My proposal keeps one tested anchor and tests two new players, which maximizes what we learn from this mission. I am not dismissing Felix's concern — I am asking the group whether the urgency to swap Amara for Arjun has a solid basis, or whether it is just a preference for familiarity. Elena, how do you read Felix's concern about Amara?

Isha asked how I read Felix’s concern about Amara. I read it as a fair question, but not as a concrete reason to remove Amara. Amara’s earlier approval was consistent with the public reasoning: the Mission 1 team was small, clearly explained, and no one had surfaced a specific suspicion. Being ready to vote is not by itself an Evil signal, and treating it as one would make ordinary confidence look suspicious. The current proposal keeps one Mission 1 anchor and tests two players who have not yet submitted cards, which is useful new information. Replacing Amara with Arjun would return to two already-tested Mission 1 members and reduce what we learn from Mission 2. I do not see enough evidence to support the swap, and I am inclined to approve Isha, Felix, and Amara.

Elena's answer to Isha doesn't address my concern. Confidence about a clean proposal isn't the issue for me. The issue is that Amara is on a three-person Mission 2 team where a single Fail card ends the mission, and nothing in the discussion gives anyone a reason to trust her with that card. I'm not willing to submit a card on a team that depends on her being Good. I can vouch only for myself. Arjun, you argued that keeping a Mission 1 member is more interpretable, and I think that point holds now. A team of Arjun, Isha, and Felix keeps a tested anchor and still tests one new player, while removing the slot I can't trust. I can't approve Isha, Felix, and Amara as drafted. Arjun, would you accept Arjun, Isha, and Felix as the Mission 2 team, or do you see a concrete problem with that swap?

Felix, yes: I would accept Arjun, Isha, and Felix. I know I am Good, and keeping both Mission 1 members gives us a more interpretable result than adding two untested players. A successful Mission 1 does not clear Isha, and I cannot vouch for Felix, but I see no concrete reason to prefer Amara over either of them. I remain inclined to reject the current draft.

Felix, you have made your position clear, and Arjun has signaled he would accept Arjun, Isha, and Felix. I want to be honest about my reasoning before I revise. My original proposal tested two untested players, which I still think is information-efficient. Amara's eagerness to approve Mission 1 is not, on its own, evidence of Evil — Good players can be confident too. But I recognize that Felix, you are firmly unwilling to approve the current team, and Arjun is also inclined to reject it. As leader, I would rather field a team that can pass than force a rejection that costs us one of five rejection chances on this mission. I am considering revising to Arjun, Isha, and Felix. Felix, if I make that revision, can you commit to approving it? I need a clear answer before I decide, because swapping without your commitment would leave us no better off than where we stand now.

Isha, to answer your question directly: yes, I will approve Arjun, Isha, and Felix as the Mission 2 team if you revise to it. I cannot approve Isha, Felix, and Amara. With a threshold of one Fail card, one untrusted slot can end the mission, and I am not willing to submit a card on a team that depends on Amara being Good. Her quick approval of Mission 1 was not the problem by itself. The problem is that after Felix raised a concern about her, she pushed for a vote and dismissed the concern without new reasoning, and nothing since has given me a reason to trust her with a Fail card. Isha, I respect your argument for testing new players, but a team with two Mission 1 members and one new player is the one I can back. I can vouch only for myself, so I will not claim more than that about anyone else. If Isha revises to Arjun, Isha, and Felix, I will vote to approve it.

I want to respond to Felix directly, since my name is on the block here. Felix's case for removing me comes down to two things: that I approved Mission 1 quickly, and that when he later raised a concern about me, I 'pushed for a vote' and 'dismissed it without new reasoning.' Let me look at what actually happened. Mission 1 was proposed with clear reasoning, no concrete suspicion was raised by anyone, and I stated my position openly, including that I had nothing against anyone at the table. That is not suspicious behavior — it is the same position Felix himself took, since he also approved that team. His turn against me only began when Isha put me on this proposed team and left him to argue for himself. That timing is worth noticing: my behavior became a problem exactly when we began competing for the same slot.

Now to the substance. Felix says he cannot trust me with a Fail card because nothing in the discussion gives a reason to trust me. But apply that standard evenly. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, yet as Arjun correctly noted, that clears no one — Evil can play Success to blend in. By Felix's own logic, Arjun is exactly as untested as I am. There is no evidence-based distinction between us. The only thing distinguishing Arjun from me in this discussion is that Arjun has personally lobbied, twice, to be put on this team, and Felix has now endorsed that swap. A team revised under these circumstances would be one where two players negotiated themselves onto the mission because one of them declined to trust a competitor for a slot, not because anything concrete surfaced about me. No one has pointed to a single statement I made that is inconsistent or deceptive. The case against me is entirely about tone and speed of an approval that Felix himself also cast.

Consider what the revision actually buys us. Swapping me for Arjun does not add a tested player — Arjun has submitted no more cards than I have. It does not improve interpretability in any way Felix has articulated beyond his personal comfort. What it does do is punish a player for having approved a mission that succeeded, and reward self-advocacy. If we adopt that standard, every future team selection becomes a contest of who can argue loudest for their own inclusion, and anyone who speaks confidently gets cut. That is a poor precedent for the remaining missions.

I remain willing to serve on Isha, Felix, and Amara, and I will submit my card honestly whichever way this goes. But I ask the table to weigh the actual record: no contradiction, no failed mission, no concrete accusation — just an approval that matched the group consensus at the time. I do not think that record justifies replacing me with a player who is, by everyone's own admission, exactly as unverified as I am.

Before this discussion closes, I want to put the decision in front of the leader with the record laid out plainly, because only Isha's turn remains and the choice is hers. The proposal on the table is Isha, Felix, and Amara. Felix has spent this discussion arguing that I should be replaced — not because I contradicted myself, not because a mission failed, and not because anyone identified a deceptive statement, but because I approved Mission 1 quickly and then defended myself when he turned on me. Look at the timing. Felix approved Mission 1 himself, with the same words of confidence he now treats as damning when they came from me. His concern about my behavior appeared for the first time only after Isha placed both of us on this team and we began competing for the same slot. That is not evidence. That is self-advocacy dressed up as caution. Apply Felix's own standard evenly, as I asked last turn. Everyone agrees Mission 1's success clears no one, because Evil can play Success. By that logic Arjun is exactly as untested as I am — he has submitted no more cards than I have, and no one has pointed to anything in his record either. The only thing that separates Arjun from me in this discussion is that Arjun has lobbied twice to be added to this team, and Felix endorsed the swap that benefits them both. If this table adopts the principle that a player can be removed because a rival for the slot declared them untrustworthy, then every future team becomes a contest of who argues loudest for their own inclusion, and confident players get cut on demand. That is a precedent Evil would love us to set, because it destroys the very information value that team selection is supposed to produce. What does the revision actually buy? Swapping me for Arjun does not add a tested player. It does not improve interpretability in any way Felix has articulated beyond his personal comfort. It removes a player whose entire record is: one approval consistent with unanimous group consensus, an open statement that she had nothing concrete against anyone, and a direct, factual rebuttal when accused. Nothing more. If that record justifies removal, then no Good player at this table is safe from arbitrary cuts, and the leader's job becomes impossible. Isha, you proposed this team for a clear reason: one tested anchor from a successful mission, and two fresh reads while missions remain to use that information. Your stated logic has not been contradicted — Elena agreed it was coherent, and Arjun's objection was about interpretability preference, not about anything I did. Felix committed to approving the revision, but note that he never committed to approving the original, so his willingness to vote was never actually in doubt for the team that includes him by name. The question for the revision is whether it is justified by evidence. It is not. I remain willing to serve, and

This is my final turn before Isha decides, so I will keep it short and factual. The record on me is unchanged: one approval on Mission 1 that matched the unanimous consensus of all five players, including Felix himself; an open statement that I had nothing concrete against anyone; and a direct, factual rebuttal when Felix turned on me. No one — not Felix, not Arjun, not anyone — has pointed to a single contradiction, deception, or failed mission involving me.

Felix's stated standard is that he cannot trust anyone he has no reason to trust. Applied honestly, that standard clears no one at this table: Arjun is exactly as untested as I am, and so is everyone else, because Mission 1's success proves nothing. The only thing separating Arjun from me in this discussion is that Arjun lobbied twice to be added to this team and Felix endorsed a swap that benefits them both. If we accept that a player can be cut because a rival for their slot declared them untrustworthy, we have made team selection a shouting contest and destroyed the information value of every mission that follows. That is a precedent that serves Evil, not Good.

Felix also claims he 'never committed to approving the original,' as if that were neutral. It is not. He signed his name to a team, then withdrew support the moment he and I competed for the same slot, and negotiated a replacement that puts himself and his preferred ally on the mission instead. The table should weigh that pattern when it evaluates his stated motives, which he frames as caution but which function as self-advocacy.

Isha's original reasoning stands untouched: one tested anchor from a successful mission, two fresh reads, maximum information from Mission 2. Elena called that logic coherent. Arjun's objection was a preference about interpretability, not an accusation against anyone. Felix's objection is a preference about personal comfort, not evidence. Neither justifies a revision, and a revision now would teach every future leader that a firm objection — however baseless — gets slots traded away on demand.

I remain willing to serve on Isha, Felix, and Amara, and I will submit my card honestly whichever way this goes. If Isha revises to Arjun, Isha, and Felix, I will not treat it as a verdict on my record — the record speaks for itself, and if a future mission fails, the table will know exactly whose lobbying shaped the teams. But I believe the stronger choice is to hold the original team, approve it, and let the mission result do the work that speculation cannot. Isha, you proposed this team with clear reasoning that no one has refuted on the evidence. I trust you to weigh the arguments, and whatever you decide, my position and my record are now fully on the table for everyone to judge.

Isha confirms Isha, Felix, Amara. After reviewing the full discussion, I'm keeping the original team. My reasoning for Isha, Felix, and Amara stands: one tested anchor from a successful mission and two fresh reads maximizes information from Mission 2. Amara's rebuttal is factually sound — Arjun is exactly as untested as she is, and no one has identified a single contradiction in her record. Felix's objection, while sincere, rests on personal comfort rather than evidence, and that standard would cut any player at this table. The team commands a majority with Elena's and Amara's support alongside mine, so I hold the lineup and take the mission result as the real evidence we need.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).

Felix proposes Felix, Isha. I'm proposing Felix and Isha for Mission 3. Mission 2 failed with Amara on the team, so I'm keeping Amara and Elena off this mission. Isha has been on a successful Mission 1 and hasn't been raised as suspicious, and with only two Evil players in this five-player game, I trust Isha and myself for this two-person team.

Mission 2 failed with exactly one Fail card, and the team was Isha, Felix, and Amara. I know I am Good and I submitted Success, so the Fail came from Felix or Amara. Felix's proposal of Felix and Isha excludes Amara, which is consistent with his stated suspicion of her, but it also keeps Felix himself on the team, and Felix was one of the two players with access to that Fail card. I want to be fair: Felix voted reject on Mission 2, and Amara voted approve, but a vote is not a card — either could have submitted the Fail once the team passed. So excluding Amara while retaining Felix is not an evidence-based distinction; it is a preference. That said, I am not ready to accuse Felix either, because Amara's eagerness in the Mission 1 discussion and her push toward a vote do give a coherent reason to keep her off this mission if the group reads it that way. What I want on the record is that a two-person team of Felix and Isha means the mission result will be maximally interpretable: if it succeeds, we bank mission 3 with two players I can reason about; if it fails, and I know I submitted Success, the table will know exactly where the Fail came from, which is valuable information we would otherwise lack. I am inclined to approve this team, but I want Felix to address the point directly, since he is the other half of this proposal.

Isha, thank you for asking me directly. I can only vouch for my own card. I submitted Success on Mission 2, so the Fail came from either Amara or Isha. I have no reason to believe you played Fail, and your statements across Missions 1 and 2 have been consistent and open. I rejected the Mission 2 team because Amara was on it. She pushed the group toward a vote after I raised a concern about her, and she has offered nothing concrete to answer that concern beyond defending her approval. Excluding Amara from Mission 3 is the choice I can stand behind. Isha and I are the only two players I can speak for, and I am comfortable approving Felix and Isha for Mission 3 on that basis. Arjun, if you have a specific objection to this two-person team, please state it before the vote.

Mission 2 failed with exactly one Fail card on Isha, Felix, and Amara. Felix now proposes Felix and Isha, excluding Amara. From the public record, that does not isolate the failure source: it retains two of the three players who had access to the Fail card and removes the third. Felix's and Isha's statements that they submitted Success are claims, not evidence. I am not accusing either of them, but I am not ready to treat this pair as more interpretable than the Mission 2 team that already failed. If this team fails, we learn one of Felix or Isha played Fail, but we already knew the Fail was among those three; if it succeeds, it does not clear Amara or resolve the original uncertainty. Arjun, you used interpretability as your standard against the previous team: do you see a concrete reason this pair is more trustworthy than keeping one Mission 2 member and testing one fresh player?

Elena, I do not see a concrete reason to trust Felix and Isha as a pair over a team containing me. Mission 2's failure places at least one Evil player among Isha, Felix, and Amara, and the successful Mission 1 does not clear Isha. I know I am Good, so I would prefer a team of Arjun and Isha: it repeats the successful pair, though even that success is not proof that Isha is Good. I am inclined to reject Felix and Isha.

Felix's proposal excludes me, and I want to answer it on the record, because his reasoning does not survive scrutiny. He has told the table he submitted Success on Mission 2. I am telling you plainly: I also submitted Success. I have nothing to hide about my card, and my record — one unanimous approval on Mission 1, consistent statements ever since — matches it. If both of us are telling the truth, then the Fail card came from Isha. I am not accusing Isha, whose statements have been open and coherent; I am pointing out that Felix's certainty about me is built on nothing, while the actual fact is that the Fail is among the three of us, and only one of us is misrepresenting their card.

Now look at Felix's behavior, because it is the most anomalous pattern at this table. He voted to reject the Mission 2 team even though he was on it. He then negotiated himself onto this proposal and excluded the one player who voted to approve that team. Rejecting a mission you are serving on is not caution — it is a player who wanted the team to fail so he could reshape the next one around himself. That is exactly the move that serves Evil, and he has dressed it up as distrust of me.

Finally, this two-person team isolates nothing. If it succeeds, we learn almost nothing new; if it fails, Felix and Isha will simply trade accusations, and we will be no closer to the truth than we are now. A better team tests someone new or includes me, so the result actually resolves something. Felix, you have now rejected a team you were on, lobbied for your own inclusion twice, and excluded the player who voted against your rejection — all while claiming the mantle of caution. Explain to the table why we should accept the judgment of a player whose every action in this game has benefited Felix.

Amara, you asked me to explain, so here it is. I submitted Success on Mission 2, and I know that from my own card. Mission 2 failed with exactly one Fail card among Isha, Felix, and Amara. Isha has said she submitted Success, and I trust that. Amara, you say you also played Success, which means the Fail came from Isha, but you cannot ask the table to accept your card claim while we also question Isha's. I can only vouch for myself and Isha, and my concern about Amara is concrete. She pushed the group toward a vote after I raised a concern about her, and she defended that approval without answering the concern itself. I rejected the Mission 2 team because Amara was on it. Excluding her from this two-person team is not an evidence-free preference; it removes the one player whose account of Mission 2 does not hold together. Arjun, you have asked for a team that is interpretable. Felix and Isha is the pair where the Mission 2 Fail is not left among three untrusted candidates. Arjun, what concrete fact would move you from rejecting Felix and Isha to approving it?

Felix, a concrete reason to change my mind would be credible evidence distinguishing you from Amara as the source of the Mission 2 Fail. Your rejection of that team is relevant, but it does not prove your card. Nor does Amara’s defense of herself prove she played Fail. I know I am Good, and I submitted Success on Mission 1, so I still prefer Arjun and Isha, the pair that succeeded. I remain inclined to reject Felix and Isha.

Mission 2's fail card came from Felix or Amara — I know I submitted Success, so one of them is lying about their card. Felix claims Success, Amara claims Success. I need to weigh their behavior, and here is what I see.

Amara raised a critical point I want the table to notice: Felix voted REJECT on Mission 2 while being on that team. A Good player who intends to submit Success and believes in the mission would vote approve. Rejecting your own team while serving on it is the most anomalous action anyone has taken in this game. If Felix was uncomfortable with Amara, the natural response as a team member who planned to play Success would be to approve the team and play honestly, then reassess after the result. Voting reject instead signals either a desire to prevent the mission from passing or a strategy to reshape the next proposal around himself — both of which serve Evil.

Felix's pattern since then confirms this: he proposed himself onto Mission 3, excluded the player who voted approve on Mission 2, and framed it all as caution. Amara voted approve on Mission 2 and is now being cut. That is self-advocacy, not evidence.

I am inclined to approve Felix and Isha because I know I am Good and I submitted Success on both missions — but I want the record clear that Felix's reject vote on his own team is a serious mark against him, and if this mission fails, the evidence points squarely at Felix.

Isha, you asked me to address my reject vote directly. I rejected the Mission 2 team because Amara was on it, and I said so at the time. That was a judgment about who was on the team, not a plan to make the mission fail, and I still submitted Success. I cannot prove my card to anyone, but I am stating it plainly. Isha has said she submitted Success, and I trust her account. That leaves the Fail with Amara or me, and I know my card. Amara's claim that the Fail must be Isha's contradicts Isha's own statement, and it is a deflection. Amara also tried to turn my reject vote into evidence against me, but she was the player who pushed the table toward a vote after I raised a concern about her, and she has answered that concern only by restating her approval. Arjun, Elena: this is a two-person team, smaller than the three-person team that failed, so it puts fewer unverified cards on a mission. I am not asking the table to accept my word alone. I am asking that Amara not be on a mission where one Fail card decides the outcome.

Felix's proposal of Felix and Isha does not deserve approval, and I want to lay out exactly why before anyone votes. The Mission 2 Fail came from Felix, Isha, or me. I submitted Success. Isha has stated she submitted Success. Felix claims he submitted Success. Felix's team keeps two of the three candidates together and calls that interpretability — it is the opposite. If it succeeds, we learn nothing we do not already know, because two Success claims were already on the table and neither is proven. If it fails, Felix and Isha will simply repeat their claims at each other, and the table will be exactly where it is now. Compare a team of Amara and Isha: it directly tests my claim against Felix's. If it succeeds, I am cleared and the Fail was Felix's. If it fails, I am finished, my record is exposed as false, and Isha is vindicated. One of these two outcomes resolves something real; Felix's proposal resolves nothing in either branch.

Now look again at the pattern behind this proposal. Felix rejected a team he was serving on. He then negotiated himself onto the next proposal, excluded the one player who voted to approve that team, and framed all of it as caution. 1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
